verified.inter_turn_gap:
Fixed and deterministic. The next request launches once more than num_users/qps seconds have passed since the previous launch (checked every 0.1 s), so think time = period minus response time. If the previous response is still running, the next request waits for it and the script logs 'unable to fit the QPS requirement'. There is no distribution and no tool time. Periods derived from the formula: README 10/0.5 = 20 s; run_single.sh 150 s down to 13.6 s; run.sh 3200 s down to 78 s; run_aws.sh 2600 s down to 63.4 s. I re-simulated the step logic in virtual time with --time 100:
- run.sh at qps 0.1: about 11 requests in total, 1 per user.
- run.sh at qps 1.3: about 144 requests, 1 per user.
- run.sh at qps 4.1: about 455 requests, at most 2 per user.
- run_aws.sh at qps 4.1: at most 2 per user.
- run_single.sh at qps 1.1: up to 8 per user.
So in the long-gap settings each user sends at most one request in the measured window.
verified.turns_per_session: --num-rounds: README 5; run.sh 10; run_single.sh 20; run_aws.sh 20; warmup 2. With the default ramp-up, the initial N users start partway through a conversation (question_id = int(offset/gap)+1) and send between 0 and R-1 requests. Only users who join after t=0 run all R rounds. With --time 100, the production-stack scripts cut every session short, as described under inter_turn_gap.
verified.context_tokens: The shared system prompt (--shared-system-prompt 1000 in all examples) plus the per-user history (--user-history-prompt: 2000 in the README, 20000 in all production-stack scripts). Both are built as space-separated 'hi' words, so the token counts are approximate. They are prepended only when a session's chat history is empty, which includes a ramped-up user's first request. The user id comes after the system prompt. So about 1k tokens form a prefix shared by all users, and about 20k tokens are unique to each user. Each later round adds a question of about 20 tokens and an answer of up to 100 tokens. By my derivation, context grows about 120 tokens per round, reaching about 23k tokens by round 20 in the production-stack settings.

verified.kv_mechanism_relevance:
- Each user's gap is periodic and deterministic, so every session's next launch time is fully predictable. That suits timer-driven prefetch, or a TTL or pin set to the per-user period. The server is told nothing about the schedule except the x-user-id header, which the LMCache copy always sends.
- The 1k-token system prompt is a global shared prefix, which tests prefix pinning.
- By my derivation, 20k-token per-user contexts across 260–320 users add up to about 5.5–6.7M tokens of KV, far more than HBM. This makes it a canonical capacity-bound tiering test.
- run.sh and run_aws.sh first run a warmup ('precompute KV and store inside CPU mem') with the same user ids. The measured 100 s window therefore mostly tests reloading each user's first request from the CPU tier. It barely tests reuse within a session or growth of context across rounds, since each user sends 1–2 requests.
- To study eviction as the gap grows, with context growing over many rounds, --time must be at least about (R-1)*N/qps, possibly with --disable-ramp-up (LMCache copy only).

result.corrections: 1) arrival_or_rate: 'interval: 60.0' is NOT a Poisson inter-arrival parameter. In inference-perf, LoadConfig.interval is defined as 'Seconds to wait between stages.' So the setup is 8 stages of 60 s each with a 60 s pause between them. The guide's own phrase '60-second Poisson interval' is loose wording; the record repeated it without checking. Also, the PoissonLoadTimer draws a Poisson count per 1-second window and spaces those requests evenly inside the window. It does not draw exponential inter-arrival gaps. 2) inter_turn_gap / reuse: prompts are not picked at random for each request. The 1250 prompts are shuffled once with a seeded RNG (rng.permutation), then walked in order (data_index % 1250). run_stage calls get_data() fresh for each stage, so every stage replays the same shuffled order from index 0 and sends int(rate*duration) requests (300/600/1200/2400 at 5/10/20/40 QPS). Only the 40 QPS stage wraps past one full pass (about 1.9 passes). This is the current main source; the version used for the June 2026 run is not stated. 3) concurrent_sessions: 'in-flight is not capped' is wrong. The profile sets neither num_workers nor worker_max_concurrency, so the inference-perf defaults apply: worker_max_concurrency=100 in-flight per worker × num_workers=CPU count. Dispatch is open-loop, but that semaphore caps in-flight requests. 4) kv results: TTFT is -55.2% (not -55%) at 5 QPS. The record left out the 40 QPS row (-76.3% mean TTFT). At 5 QPS, E2E latency got worse (+7.5% mean, +35.7% P90). Only 4 of the 8 profile stages (5, 10, 20, 40 QPS) are reported. 5) Minor: the profile template has 'server: type: vllm' even though it is used for the SGLang runs, so the harness presumably overrides it. The guide's default table lists '100 GB CPU Cache Offload Size', but the SGLang result used --hicache-size 200 (200 GiB/replica). All other fields check out word for word: 250 groups, 5 prompts/group, 16000/256/256 tokens, multi-turn off, stage rates, 16×H100 / 8 servers / TP=2 / Qwen3-32B / SGLang v0.5.13.post1, GPU/CPU cache token counts, 4,640,000-token working set (=250×16000 + 1250×512), and the TTFT numbers at 10 and 20 QPS. Year 2026 is confirmed (results file committed June 25, 2026, PR #1921).

result.corrections:
I checked the claims against the master branch at commit 94f6046 (2026-07-12): README.md, trace_replay_tester.py and docs/trace_replay_tester.md, plus the LMCache blog page. I also recomputed the stats from all 739 trace JSONs. Every README statistic in the record matches exactly (for example think time 0/6/10/30/78,638/199; requests per trace 3/19/48/101/1,178/80). Corrections:

(1) OUTPUT TOKENS: the blog gives no median output of about 169. The number 169 appears only as `"out":169` in one example trace JSON snippet. Mark the blog output median "not stated". The README values (P10 103, P50 218, P90 937, mean 446) are correct.

(2) TTFT-GATED RAMP: the record says "p95/avg TTFT under --max-ttft". The code defaults --ttft-metric to "avg" (choices max/avg/p95). The value used is a rolling mean over --ttft-window=3 assessment periods of 30 s each. A user is added only with at least 20% headroom, so the rolling TTFT must be below 0.8 x max_ttft. Each period adds 1+int(headroom_pct/15) users. Adding is also blocked while any user is rate-limited, when the working set exceeds 90% of --max-working-set-tokens, or when --max-new-tokens-per-period (default 500000) is used up. The blog says the ramp runs on "p95 TTFT", but its reproduce command does not set --ttft-metric, so under the current code the default avg would apply. The blog's SLOs were 60 s (stress) and 30 s (base), not the 2.0 s default.

(3) --cache-max-age: the code settles it. It only calls prune_old_blocks() on the tester's own client-side working-set tracker (block_last_access), and that tracker feeds only working-set metrics and ramp gating. It is never sent to the server, so it is not a server TTL or pinning parameter.

(4) SUB-AGENTS: spawn_subagent() inserts each sub-agent into self.users, so sub-agents count as live users against --max-users.

(5) The blog's "peak concurrent users plateaued at 4-8" is a verbatim quote, but it contradicts the blog's own base-load table: peak users were 2 (Vanilla), 8 (HBM-PC) and 3 (LMCache).

(6) docs/trace_replay_tester.md is out of date and disagrees with the code: it gives --ttft-metric default p95, --max-delay 60.0 and --max-concurrent-requests 50. The code says avg, 600.0 and 0. The record's code-based defaults are correct.

(7) The record's argparse quotes were joined onto one line. The source spreads them over several lines; exact line fragments are given below.

(8) Missing context on turns: --max-context filters out traces whose first request is over the limit, and a session ends ("truncated") at its first request over the limit. My own recomputation, which the source does not state: at the 128k default, 588 traces are eligible with median 38 turns (P25 17, P75 65). At 100k (blog stress) it is 541 traces, median 26. At 32k (blog base) it is 397 traces, median 3. So the blog's base run had very short sessions.

(9) Also computed from the traces, not stated in the README: think time P90 is 154 s, about 75% of gaps are 30 s or less, and about 4.1% are over the 600 s --max-delay cap. The blog gives a different conversation duration (median 60 min, P75 163) from the README (62 / 141).

verified.concurrent_sessions: LIVE USERS (sessions held open across think time): --start-users defaults to 1 and the tester ramps toward --max-users (default 50). Sub-agents are added as separate live users and count against --max-users. Users are added once per 30-s assessment period, gated by a rolling avg TTFT (default metric avg, not p95) that must be below 0.8 x --max-ttft (default 2.0 s). Adding is also blocked by rate-limited users, the working-set cap and the 500k per-period new-token budget. --recycle replaces completed users. README example: start 5, max 50. verified.arrival_or_rate: Closed loop per user: each user's next request fires after the previous one completes plus the replayed delay. The number of users grows adaptively each 30 s assessment period. There is no fixed request rate. Throughput reported is steady state within the TTFT SLO.

result.corrections:
I re-read the files from raw.githubusercontent.com (main branch) along with benchmarks/benchmark.py, generator/workload_generator/workload_generator.py, sample_request.py, client/client.py, client/utils.py and scenarios/kvcache/README.md. Every numeric value in the record is in the source. The corrections below are about what those values mean, plus details the record left out.
(1) context_tokens: synthetic_multiturn prompt_length 80 / prompt_std 472 is the length of each turn's new prompt (drawn from a Pareto distribution in ParetoSampler). It is not the size of the accumulated context. Context grows because the client's prepare_prompt/update_response prepends the full session history (user and assistant messages) to every sessioned request. Agent prompt sizes: plan = initial_prompt_tokens + turn*context_growth_tokens, followup = plan + tool_count*tool_result_tokens. Session history is prepended on top of these.
(2) inter_turn_gap: think_time_ms applies only between turns ('if turn + 1 < turn_count'), never after the last turn. Inside a turn, the gap from plan to followup is the slowest of the parallel tool calls, including a retry (retry_probability 0.1, max_tool_retries 1). The generator computes timestamps in advance from an assumed model_latency_ms (example [100,400], default [50,150]), not from measured latency. The stock client holds each later request in a session until the previous one finishes, then sleeps until the request's scheduled timestamp. The gap actually seen is therefore max(0, scheduled time - completion time). For the chat multi-turn workload no gap is stated. Mechanically, each Poisson arrival (rate target_qps) goes to a random session among the first max_concurrent_sessions sessions still open. With QPS 1 and N=2, the per-session gap averages about 2 s (my derivation, not stated).
(3) concurrent_sessions: in the generator, max_concurrent_sessions picks a session uniformly from the first min(remaining, N) sessions, so at most N sessions interleave in the generated trace. Its CLI default is 1 ('Maximum number of overlapping sessions'). The config.yaml value of 2 is correct. The agent generator has no cap. My simulation of the example agent config with 2000 sessions gave about 5 live sessions on average and a peak of 15; this is derived (Little's law, 0.5/s times about 10 s per session), not stated. The client_max_concurrent_sessions null default is correct.
(4) turns_per_session: each agent turn issues two model requests (plan and followup), so a session sends 2x turns requests. Multiturn turn counts are drawn as int(Normal(3.55, 2.89)) and clamped to at least 1. The CLI defaults for num_sessions are mean 10, std 10, against 1000 in config.yaml.
(5) kv_mechanism_relevance overstated a point. The README says 'Existing benchmark clients therefore remain compatible and ignore the structural events', so the stock client does not use the tool, wait or join events. A scheduler hint would need a custom consumer. Also, the prompt factory puts the session and node IDs at the very start of every agent prompt ('Anonymous synthetic Agent session {session_id}, node {node_id}.'). Two agent prompts therefore share only a few tokens, and prefix reuse across turns comes only from the history the client prepends.
(6) hardware_model: the README's agent example uses tokenizer Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, and the client README serves deepseek-llm-7b-chat on vLLM with --max-model-len 4096. No GPU is named. The 'Coming Soon!' quote is confirmed in benchmarks/scenarios/kvcache/README.md.
(7) The evidence quote 'constant: target_qps: 1 ... max_concurrent_sessions: 2' was shortened with an ellipsis. The full block is quoted below.
(8) year: the GitHub API hit its rate limit, so I could not check commit dates. '2025-2026' is plausible but unverified.

result.corrections:
I checked every field against the arXiv v7 PDF (arXiv:2511.02230v7 [cs.OS], 8 Sep 2026; full text extracted) and the repo README at github.com/Hanchenli/vllm-continuum. The core numbers are correct. These fields needed correction or qualification:

1. The 0.13 JPS rate. The record says this is the only rate in the text and that it belongs to the "turn-scaling ablation". The text actually states 0.13 JPS twice: once for the batch-size and chunk-size sensitivity study (Fig. 13) and once for turn scaling (Fig. 14). Both are in Section 6.3 "Sensitivity Analysis", not the ablation. The real ablation (Fig. 16) states no rate; its ticks are about 0.04–0.10 JPS for SWE-Bench and about 0.8–3.2 JPS for BFCL.

2. "Open-loop" is not in the paper. It only says "using poisson distribution for the arrival pattern of agent programs". Program arrivals are open-loop Poisson. Turns inside a program are closed-loop: the next request is sent when the tool returns.

3. The number of live sessions and the in-flight concurrency are not stated. What is stated: Fig. 13 varies the max batch size (in-flight cap) over 16/32/64/128/256 at 0.13 JPS, and the default is not stated. The repo README (not the paper) gives an example of a fixed-concurrency mode, "--workers 64", and a Poisson mode, "--jps 1.0".

4. Turn scaling. The record leaves out the turn counts the paper gives: 1x = 10.9, 2x = 20.8, 3x = 30.8, 4x = 40.7, 5x = 50.6 turns.

5. Tool time. Table 2 labels the column only "Tool Time(ms)" and never says per call. Per call is the likely reading, given about 11 turns per program. The paper also never says explicitly that tool durations are replayed as sleeps; it only calls these "trace replay experiments". Online, the system measures tool time as the server-side interval between one request finishing and the next request from the same program arriving.

6. Tokens per program. Table 2 does not say whether "Token Per Program" means the final accumulated context or the total tokens processed. The BFCL scaling is quoted exactly below. Its wording ("to fit at least 100 request") is garbled in the source, and it is unclear whether Table 2 shows BFCL before or after the 0.4 scaling.

7. Workload type. Section 3.1 says 100 traces each were collected for SWE-Bench and BFCL, using GPT-5. The paper says "two collected workloads running GPT-5" but then lists three datasets, so it is unclear whether the OpenHands traces are also GPT-5.

8. KV mechanism nuances. A pin is released only when its TTL has expired and its program_id is not in the waiting queue. Waiting-queue priority is: preempted requests first, then requests still within their TTL, then program-level arrival order. When memory is exhausted, the deadlock breaker unpins the program with the latest arrival first. The TTL is chosen by maximizing P(τ,f)·(T·η + Prefill-Reload) − τ over the empirical per-tool CDF. It falls back to global tool records, and to a fixed T_default when there are at most K=100 records. The paper describes no prefetch or promotion from DRAM during tool time. The released code is "without the estimation in the paper".

9. Minor points. Section 1 says tool calls can be "≤ 2s". The real SWE-Bench-Verified run compares against SGLang 0.5.5.post3 and Dynamo 0.7.0.post1 (1P1D), and its model is not stated. The SSD tier uses 400G and 800G on Llama-8B with a B200.

The venue, year, hardware and tick-range fields are confirmed as written.

verified.kv_mechanism_relevance: Continuum pins KV in GPU memory during tool calls with a TTL, deciding per request (τ can be 0). τ* = argmax over τ of P(τ,f)·(T·η + Prefill-Reload(r)) − τ. P is the empirical CDF of recorded durations for tool f. T is a sliding-window average of queueing delay for evicted requests. η = −Corr(k, N−k) is the 'memoryfulness' factor. Prefill-Reload comes from offline profiling and depends on whether CPU offload is on. Fallbacks: global tool records, or a fixed T_default (derived assuming Exp(1) tool times and η = 1) when there are at most K=100 records. A pin is released only when the TTL has expired and the program is not in the waiting queue. It is also released when the program ends, or by the deadlock breaker, which unpins the program with the latest arrival first. Waiting-queue priority: preempted requests, then requests within TTL, then program-level FCFS. The paper argues that per-turn queueing after eviction adds up across turns even with fast asynchronous LMCache reload, which InferCept's Preserve ignores. The gain holds on top of DRAM and SSD offload, and grows with turn count (Fig. 14). The paper describes no prefetch or promotion from DRAM or SSD during tool idle time. The public code omits the TTL estimation.

verified.kv_mechanism_relevance: Program-level attained-service scheduling: PLAS for single-threaded programs, ATLAS for multi-threaded ones. Preemption causes GPU↔CPU KV swapping. Autellix cuts the number of swaps with multi-step scheduling (the scheduler runs once every N decode steps and overprovisions requests already on the GPU). It speeds up each swap with a gather-to-contiguous-buffer kernel (up to 18x fewer swaps, 3-7x lower swap time). Autellix explicitly does NOT do proactive or next-iteration prefetch, because it is synchronous. It has no idle-time prefetch and no TTL or pinning during tool calls, and Continuum calls it end-of-turn eviction. The locality-aware load balancer sends calls of 2048 tokens or fewer to the least-loaded engine and pins longer calls to their program's engine. Within a program the prefix hit rate is above 90%, while across programs only the system prompt is shared. Continuum (arXiv 2511.02230) reimplements it as Autellix+ with LMCache CPU offload.

result.corrections:
I checked the raw docs, the datagen and loadgen source, and the profile YAMLs from both repos at HEAD on 2026-09-23 (inference-perf dd4434eb, llm-d-benchmark 3feb44bf). Every number in the record is present in its source, but several meanings were wrong.

(1) concurrent_sessions was wrong. concurrency_level is NOT the number of live conversations. It is the in-flight request cap: each worker takes a Semaphore permit before the request waits on its conversation's session lock, and it keeps that permit through the tool-call sleep. The number of live conversations is num_conversations: 200 in the quick start, 50 in interactive-chat and 40 in agentic_code_generation. Requests go out round-robin over all conversations. The two numbers match only when num_conversations == concurrency_level, which the datagen docstring recommends. The profiles do not follow that advice at their lower stages. For example, interactive-chat at concurrency 10 keeps 50 contexts live.

(2) turns_per_session needed a caveat. LocalUserSession.clear_instances() runs between stages, and every stage restarts at data_index 0, which is turn 0. So the turns a conversation actually runs in a stage is about num_requests/num_conversations: 2000/200 = 10 in the quick start (against a configured mean of 38), 300/50 = 6 in interactive-chat, and 100/40 to 800/40 (2.5 to 20) in agentic_code_generation. The configured means are never reached within a stage.

(3) Nominal lognormal means are misleading once clipping applies. The sampler moment-matches mean and std, then clips to [min, max]. I simulated this (my own simulation, not a source statement):
- agentic turns (mean 540, std 48600, clipped to [1, 3000]): effective median about 6, mean about 153.
- agentic tool latency (mean 15, std 55, clipped to [1, 100]): median about 4 s, mean about 12 s, p90 about 32 s.
- interactive-chat tool latency: median about 34 s, mean about 45 s.
- docs example tool latency: median about 6 s, mean about 8 s.
Sampled values are rounded to whole numbers.

(4) The quick-start YAML has no tool_call_latency_sec, so its turns run back to back (0 s gap). The 8 s lognormal is a separate docs snippet.

(5) Context cap: the docs say the session "is reset" above about 225K tokens. In the current code, max_model_len defaults to 225000 and LocalUserSession.update_context drops the oldest history turns when the prompt goes over it, rather than resetting. agentic_code_generation sets max_model_len 262144, so its dynamic-prompt maximum of 990000 cannot be reached.

(6) The OTel recorded gaps (wait_ms) are capped by max_wait_ms, which defaults to 15000 ms.

(7) The quote 'Each slot (preferred_worker_id) maps to one concurrent conversation' comes from the conversation_replay_datagen.py docstring, not from docs/conversation_replay.md.

(8) Worker settings the record left out: interactive-chat uses num_workers 1. agentic_code_generation uses num_workers 8 and worker_max_concurrency 1000.

(9) Models: none of these sources state hardware. The inference-perf workload-catalog copies of these profiles name google/gemma-3-1b-it (interactive-chat) and Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct (code-generation). The llm-d-benchmark versions are model-agnostic.

These fields were confirmed as the record had them: all distribution parameters, the stage concurrency and num_requests lists, the shared_prefix_multi_turn_chat settings, agent_llm_traces_v2 at 64 sessions, the guidellm multi-turn settings, and the OTel session_rate 2.0 and concurrent_sessions 4 examples.

verified.kv_mechanism_relevance: This source directly models tool-execution idle windows: the sleep is async, so 'the GPU remains free to serve other concurrent conversations during the wait'. That window is when a KV tier could prefetch the next turn's prefix, and when a TTL or pin must keep that KV resident. Two points matter for sizing: the live KV footprint equals num_conversations contexts, while the in-flight cap (concurrency_level) includes conversations that are sleeping. The profiles give three gap scales: about 6-8 s tool calls (docs), about 4 s median and 12 s mean for agentic code, and about 34 s median and 45 s mean for interactive chat. OTel replay caps recorded gaps at 15 s by default. Per-stage session clearing limits how much context builds up unless num_requests is at least num_conversations × turns.

result.corrections:
1) Wrong paper version. The record says NeurIPS 2025, which is right: the camera-ready reads "39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)". But its content comes from arXiv v1 (2507.07400v1, "Preprint. Under review."), and the NeurIPS camera-ready evaluation is different:
   (a) The single-workflow test with Llama-3.1-8B on an A10G (PCIe Gen1, 2 GB/s) exists only in v1. The camera-ready runs the single-workflow test only on Qwen2.5-32B on an H100. It also adds branches=1 and branches=2 variants and a vLLM baseline.
   (b) v1 describes "10 agents"; the camera-ready describes a "10-stage" workflow. With branches=2, each stage randomly picks one of two agents.
   (c) Figure numbers differ. The concurrency figure is Fig. 6 in v1 and Fig. 5 in the camera-ready. The PEER figure is Fig. 8 in v1 and Fig. 7 in the camera-ready.
   (d) The single-workflow Fixed/Dynamic/Output sweeps differ. v1 on A10G: 4096 and 8192 fixed × {32/32, 128/128, 1024/1024}. v1 on H100: 4096 and 8192 × {32/32, 256/256, 1024/1024}. Camera-ready: 4096/32/32, 4096/256/256, 8192/32/32 and 8192/256/256 only.
2) hardware_model is wrong for the concurrency test. All four concurrency configurations, Qwen2.5-32B and Llama-3.1-8B alike, ran on ONE H100: the figure caption says "on an H100", and the camera-ready says "four configurations with models Qwen2.5-32B and Llama-3.1-8B". Llama on the A10G applies only to the v1 single-workflow test. The hardware for the PEER test is not stated.
3) concurrent_sessions overstates how concurrency was chosen. The paper does not say it picked the "highest the GPU holds". It says "a proper concurrency that the GPU can accommodate without exhausting memory for prefix caching". The other numbers check out against the figure tick labels. The camera-ready adds that these workflows are sequential (branches=1), non-interacting and non-sharing.
4) turns_per_session: for the concurrency test, neither the number of agents per workflow nor the number of iterations is stated. For the PEER test, 4 agents per workflow is stated, but the number of iterations is not. In the camera-ready, the single-workflow test runs the 10-stage workflow 10 times, and that whole process is repeated 10 more times to report mean and standard deviation.
5) output_tokens: "32 up to larger values" is vague. The explicit values are 32, 128 or 1024 (v1, A10G); 32, 256 or 1024 (v1, H100); 32 or 256 (camera-ready); and 256 fixed in the concurrency test. For PEER, only a distribution is plotted (Fig. 7/8, axis 0 to 600 tokens), with no numeric summary.
6) context_tokens: "512–8192" is only a union. The fixed prefix is 512 or 1024 in the concurrency test and 4096 or 8192 in the single-workflow test.
7) inter_turn_gap: "not stated" is correct. No think time, tool time or arrival process is modeled. "Back to back" is an inference from the workflows being sequential; the paper does not say it.
8) kv_mechanism_relevance leaves out things that matter for KV tiering:
   - Status-aware scheduling: requests whose prefix is still loading are skipped. Cache nodes have four states (GPU / CPU backup / loading / offloading).
   - Prefetch starts only "if the evictable GPU memory is large enough".
   - Dynamic suffixes always get the highest eviction priority.
   - The camera-ready adds adaptive removal of fixed-prompt nodes that have not been reused beyond a threshold period.
   - When the workflow is unpredictable, the system falls back to equal priority and turns prefetch off.
   - The concurrent-prefetch cap is mentioned only for workflows with branches.

verified.concurrent_sessions: Closed batch: N independent, non-interacting, non-sharing sequential workflows (branches=1) launched at the same time on a single H100. verified.output_tokens: Equal to the dynamic length in each single-workflow setting: 32, 128 or 1024 (v1, A10G); 32, 256 or 1024 (v1, H100); 32 or 256 (camera-ready). Fixed at 256 in the concurrency test. For PEER, only a distribution is shown, with no numeric summary.

Concurrency test: both Qwen2.5-32B and Llama-3.1-8B on a single H100. PEER hardware not stated. Baselines: SGLang (GPU-only radix cache, LRU), SGLang w/ HiCache (LRU, reactive load-back, layer-wise two-stage pipeline), and vLLM (camera-ready single-workflow test only).
verified.kv_mechanism_relevance:
- Eviction: follows each agent's steps-to-execution from an Agent Step Graph, assigned per KV node on SGLang's radix tree. Shared nodes take the minimum (least evictable) priority. Dynamic suffixes always get the highest eviction priority. This replaces LRU.
- Prefetch: proactive CPU-to-GPU prefetch in background threads for agents in the next step. It overlaps with compute through full-duplex PCIe and starts only if the evictable GPU memory is large enough. When the workflow branches, all possible next agents are prefetched, up to a predefined limit on concurrent prefetches.
- Status-aware scheduling: this is the queue-aware part. Cache nodes have four states (GPU / CPU backup / loading / offloading). The scheduler skips requests whose prefix is still loading and dispatches other ready requests. Nodes that are offloading are excluded from eviction.
- Camera-ready additions: fixed-prompt nodes not reused beyond a threshold period are removed automatically, and when future steps are unpredictable the system falls back to equal priority with prefetch turned off.
- Reported result: HiCache does poorly under high concurrency, reaching 0.57x of GPU-only SGLang at 1024-token prefixes with 64 concurrent workflows. KVFlow is up to 2.19x faster than HiCache there.
- There is no pinning or TTL during tool calls, because tool calls are not modeled.

verified.kv_mechanism_relevance:
Program-aware pause/restore:
- A periodic monitor (every ∆t=5, unit not given) checks whether the summed program tokens on a backend exceed KV capacity (λmax=λmin=1).
- Tokens of acting (tool-running) programs are discounted by f(t_q)=2^−t_q, where t_q is the current tool time. Idle KV therefore gets evicted progressively instead of being pinned, as a TTL would do.
- The pause score 1/c + I(acting) prefers acting programs, then the shortest contexts, because recompute cost grows with c². Restore prefers reasoning programs, then the shortest contexts.
- A global queue restores paused programs on any DP node.

verified.kv_mechanism_relevance: GPU-only radix-tree KV cache. Eviction is LRU, least-recently-used leaf first, and nodes used by the running batch cannot be evicted. Cache-aware scheduling sorts requests by matched prefix length. The paper mentions no CPU or disk tiering, no prefetch, and no TTL or pinning for idle sessions. Production evidence: after a month in Chatbot Arena, hit rates were 52.4% for LLaVA-Next-34B and 74.1% for Vicuna-33B, with hits partly from multi-turn chat histories, cutting TTFT by 1.7× on average for Vicuna-33B.
evidence_quotes: Multi-turn chat with 4 turns, where the input of each turn is randomly sampled between 256-512 tokens. Multi-turn chat (short) means short output (4-8 tokens) and multi-turn chat (long) means long output (256-512 tokens)

For throughput, we run a sufficiently large batch of program instances to compute the maximum throughput, comparing the number of program instances executed per second (programs per second, p/s). For latency, we execute a single program at a time without batching and report the average latency for multiple instances.
We run most experiments on AWS EC2 G5 instances, which are equipped with NVIDIA A10G GPUs (24GB). We run 7B models on a single A10G GPU and larger models on multiple A10G GPUs with tensor parallelism
Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 are obtained by running Llama-7B on a single A10G (24GB) GPU.
For open-weight models, the number of parameters ranges from 7 billion to 70 billion, and we use float16 precision.

we introduce a simple LRU eviction policy that evicts the least recently used leaf first. By evicting leaves first, we enable the re-use of their common ancestors until those ancestors become leaves and are also evicted. In the continuous batching setting, we cannot evict nodes used by the currently running batch.
Sort the requests by matched prefix length and prioritize requests with longer matched prefixes.

SGLang has been deployed in Chatbot Arena [8] to serve open-weight models. Due to low traffic for some models, only one SGLang worker serves each. After one month, we observed a 52.4% RadixAttention cache hit rate for LLaVA-Next-34B [28] and 74.1% for Vicuna-33B [7]. verified.kv_mechanism_relevance: Directly relevant to KV tiering during tool calls. The Temporal Scheduler reacts to call_start and call_finish HTTP events. It offloads a stalled agent's KV to CPU only when three conditions all hold. (1) The predicted stall covers a round-trip transfer. (2) A waiting request can use the freed blocks. (3) The later upload can be prepared without displacing more important work. Algorithm 1 adds four hard rejections, including insufficient CPU capacity. Upload is gradual and predictive before the forecast completion, ranked by P_upload = importance + urgency under an upload budget that protects critical waiting requests. If the tool returns early, the upload happens immediately. Tool duration is forecast per function type as an EWMA blended with a user estimate. The Spatial Scheduler reserves HBM for critical agent types. Offload-only without agent awareness did 11,339 offloads, more than double TokenCake's swap volume. Its total latency fell from 502.2 s to 403.1 s, but its average and P90 stayed close to baseline. TokenCake cut swap volume 51% compared with offload-only. A PCIe round trip costs 15.8–79.8 ms, versus recompute that is 26.8–37.5× slower. The repo's current vLLM v0.22.0 implementation does NOT do predictive prefetching; it uses demand-triggered recovery.

result.corrections:
All the numbers the record quotes from the docs and configs are correct. I checked them against the AIPerf repo at HEAD 62510dc2 (2026-09-23): docs/tutorials/agentic-code-generator.md, configs/default.json, datasets/1k_sessions_200k_ctx/manifest.json + README.md, docs/tutorials/agentx-mvp.md and weka-trace.md, and the synthesizer/timing source. Five fields needed a correction or a change of meaning.

(1) inter_turn_gap and the KV relevance claim. The configured mixture is not what gets replayed. session_synthesizer._sample_delay_ms multiplies each sampled delay by max(0.2, 1 - 0.8*prev_input/max_prompt_tokens), so gaps shrink as context grows, down to 0.2x at full context. The 15-25 s human medians are therefore pre-scaling config values, not the gaps in the trace. Each component's 'max' is truncation by rejection resampling, not a hard clip. I ran the actual synthesizer code with seed 42 (these numbers are derived, not stated anywhere):
- default, 1000 sessions: realized delay mean 6.0 s, median 1.44 s, p90 18.2 s, p99 56.8 s.
- manifest, 1205 sessions: mean 7.5 s, median 2.0 s, p90 17.4 s, p99 87.7 s.
Delays are end-to-start: FixedScheduleStrategy schedules the next turn delay_ms after the previous request's credit returns.

(2) concurrent_sessions for Agentic Code. The tutorial does not define it, but AIPerf does elsewhere: --concurrency 'Limits concurrent sessions', and session_tree.py describes the legacy non-agentic model as holding a slot 'acquired on the root's first turn, released on the root's final turn'. So --concurrency 50 means 50 live sessions, each holding its slot across its inter-turn delays. Every turn-0 row has timestamp 0, and a trace with a timestamp is auto-promoted to fixed-schedule, where concurrency acts as a ceiling. The result is effectively a closed loop of 50 live sessions.

(3) turns_per_session. The record says 'not stated', which is literally true. Running the code with seed 42 gives:
- default: mean 15.4 turns, median 17, p10 7, max 18. 78% of sessions end by forced retire and 22% by probabilistic reset. Final-turn input averages about 148k tokens, from about 38.9k at turn 0.
- manifest: mean 11.7, median 11, p10 2, p90 23, max 34, with 69% resets.
The manifest also sets restart_initial_probability 0.3 and restart_turn_range [5,15]. The default has restart probability 0.0.

(4) context_tokens. The record left out that the manifest caps L2 at max 50000; the default's cap is 30000. The default new_tokens_per_turn has median 6000 = mean 6000, so sigma is 0 and new tokens are nearly constant. The record does not mention the bias of 1.1.

(5) AgentX details the record left out:
- The corpus is 393 traces (semianalysisai/cc-traces-weka-062126).
- Per-request max_tokens comes from the recorded 'out' field.
- --concurrency caps session trees, not requests. In-flight requests can exceed it at subagent fan-out.
- The 10 s idle cap applies to the whole system: it shifts all pending timers only when no request is active or ready. It does not shorten any single session's gap.
- Lanes start at a random point t* between 0 and 1.0 of the trace's duration, and recycled traces restart at turn 0.

verified.workload_type: Two workloads. Agentic Code: synthetic long-context coding-agent sessions written as Mooncake-trace JSONL, with layered prefixes (L1 global, L1.5 group, L2 session, L3 growing history), probabilistic resets, forced retire at max_prompt_tokens, and restart splits. AgentX MVP: replay of real Claude Code sessions from the Weka corpus (393 traces, with subagent SPAWN/JOIN trees).
verified.concurrent_sessions: Agentic Code: the examples use --concurrency 50, which caps live sessions. The tutorial itself does not define this, but AIPerf does: the timing-modes reference says '--concurrency ... Limits concurrent sessions', and a session holds its slot from first turn to final turn, including the gaps between turns (session_tree.py, legacy non-agentic path). AgentX MVP: --concurrency is the number of live session trees, 'Exactly --concurrency trees stay live at all times'. A lane keeps its slot until the root and all its subagents drain. The example uses 32. At subagent fan-out, in-flight requests can exceed 32.
verified.arrival_or_rate: Agentic Code: every turn-0 row has timestamp 0, and a trace with a timestamp is auto-promoted to fixed-schedule. With concurrency as a ceiling, sessions start whenever a slot frees up, so this is effectively a closed loop of 50 live sessions. The examples run 1000 sessions, with an optional --benchmark-duration 2400. AgentX: a closed loop of N live trees for --benchmark-duration 1800 s (900 s minimum). A lane recycles when its tree drains, and recycled traces restart at turn 0.
verified.inter_turn_gap:
Agentic Code, configured values (lognormal mixture, 70% agentic / 30% human):
- default: agentic mean 2500 ms / median 1800 ms (truncated at 10000); human mean 40000 / median 25000 (truncated at 120000); no top-level max.
- manifest: agentic mean 5000 / median 2000; human mean 30000 / median 15000; no max.
The code then scales each sample by max(0.2, 1 - 0.8*context_ratio), so gaps shrink as context grows.
Realized delays, derived by running the synthesizer with seed 42 (not stated in the docs):
- default: mean 6.0 s, median 1.44 s, p90 18.2 s, p99 56.8 s.
- manifest: mean 7.5 s, median 2.0 s, p90 17.4 s, p99 87.7 s.
Turn 0 has delay 0. Delay is end-to-start: the next turn is scheduled on credit return.
AgentX: the recorded end-to-start gaps are replayed, and per-trace and per-turn caps are forbidden. A global --system-idle-gap-cap-seconds 10 shifts all pending timers only when no request is active or ready.
verified.turns_per_session:
Agentic Code: reset-driven by default, with no fixed count. A session ends on a probabilistic reset (p = base*(1+(scaling-1)*ctx/max); default base 0.01 and scaling 1.5, manifest base 0.05), on forced retire at max_prompt_tokens, or on a restart split (manifest only: probability 0.3, split at turns 5-15). None of the docs state a turn count. Derived by running the code with seed 42:
- default: mean 15.4 turns, median 17, p10 7, max 18; 78% end by forced retire.
- manifest: mean 11.7, median 11, p10 2, p90 23, max 34.
AgentX: turns as recorded in the 393 traces; the count is not stated.
verified.context_tokens:
Default config:
- L1 global prefix: 32000 tokens.
- L1.5: 0.
- L2 session context: mean 15000 / median 5000, truncated at 30000.
- New tokens per turn: mean = median 6000, max 10000, bias 1.1.
- max_prompt_tokens 167000; block_size 512.
- Derived: turn-0 input averages about 38.9k tokens and final-turn input about 148k.
Manifest:
- L1 32000 + L1.5 10000, across 100 groups (zipf 0.6).
- L2: mean 15000 / median 5000, max 50000.
- New tokens per turn: mean 6000 / median 4000, max 50000.
- max_prompt_tokens 200000.
AgentX example: --max-context-length 128000, which filters out traces whose peak input+output exceeds 128k.
verified.output_tokens: Default generation_length: mean 1000, median 1000, max 1500. Manifest: mean 1000, median 800, max 10000. AgentX: max_tokens comes from each request's recorded 'out' field, and ignore_eos:true is locked, so the server generates the full requested length.
verified.hardware_model: The examples use Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B (Agentic Code replay) and deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro (AgentX). GPUs are not stated.
verified.kv_mechanism_relevance: The mixture separates short agentic tool gaps from long human think gaps. The human gaps are the ones long enough for HBM-to-host offload plus prefetch to pay off; short tool gaps favour keeping or pinning KV in HBM. But the synthesizer shrinks every gap by up to 5x as context grows. The realized median is only about 1.4-2.0 s, with about 10% of gaps above 17-18 s, and the largest contexts get the shortest gaps. The configured 15-25 s human medians overstate the idle windows available at high context. Session slots are held across gaps, so the whole working set of 50 (or N) sessions stays resident or must be tiered. The layered L1/L1.5/L2/L3 prefixes model global, group and per-session reuse. AgentX adds real Claude Code timing with subagent fan-out, a per-play cache-bust marker that prevents artificial cross-play prefix reuse, and a global 10 s idle-compression guard that does not shorten individual gaps while other sessions are active.

verified.venue_or_repo: arXiv 2606.00866 (v1). Authors: Tian Xia, Hanchen Li, Zhifei Li, Xiaokun Chen, Hao Kang, Yifan Qiao, Yi Xu, Ion Stoica. Built on ThunderAgent and SGLang v0.5.10 with HiCache.
verified.workload_type: A self-collected replay of Claude Code sessions: claude-sonnet-4-6 at the default high effort level, run on the SWE-bench Pro test split. Of the first 200 tasks, 186 gave complete traces. Each program is replayed as a sequence of (input length, output length, tool-call duration) tuples. Parallel tool calls are merged into a single gap equal to the longest call.
verified.concurrent_sessions: Live sessions in a closed loop: 20, 50 and 80 concurrent programs per DP replica, so the DP=3 H200 configuration runs 3× those totals. Each slot replays one trace and starts a new trace from the corpus as soon as it finishes. Runs last a fixed 1 hour. A slot counts toward concurrency while it sleeps through a tool call, so the number of requests in flight at any moment is lower. At 20 programs the working set fits in the CPU tier (87–96% cache hit rate). At 50 and 80 programs the aggregate KV cache exceeds combined GPU and CPU capacity.
verified.arrival_or_rate: Not applicable: closed loop with one program per slot, replayed 'under identical arrival patterns' across systems. No open-loop arrival rate is given.
verified.inter_turn_gap: The replayed gap is the recorded tool-call duration, applied as a sleep, with no separate think time. Durations are heavy-tailed, from hundreds of ms (file reads) up to minutes (human input, subagents). The Fig. 3 caption says the distribution spans more than three orders of magnitude. verified.kv_mechanism_relevance: Idleness is the share of time spent in tool calls (Acting) over the last k=5 inference–tool-call cycles, ι = T_acting / (T_reasoning + T_acting). Placement is sticky across three tiers: GPU queue (HBM), CPU queue (DRAM), and a global Waiting queue whose KV is discarded and recomputed. When GPU is over capacity, the most idle Acting programs are demoted first. When space frees up, CPU programs whose tool call has completed are promoted first, lowest idleness first. The scheduler tick is 5 s. Typed hints (busy/idle/inactive) are stamped onto HiCache radix-tree nodes. On GPU the eviction order is inactive, then idle, then busy. When multiple tool calls execute in parallel, we treat them as a single gap whose duration is the maximum of the individual durations.
The distribution spans several orders of magnitude, from hundreds of milliseconds for file reads to up to minutes for human input or subagent invocations.

For a program in a short tool-call gap, this transfer cost can exceed the gap itself, making offloading counterproductive.

I read the full arXiv v1 text in HTML and PDF form, including the figure axis labels. Most fields hold up. These need fixing:
(1) concurrent_sessions: the paper does not tie "100 concurrent requests" to the multi-engine test. That quote, "(720 to 910 seconds under 100 concurrent requests)", comes from §5.8, the scheduling-policy debugging case with mini-SWE-agent (Fig. 15 sweeps 60/80/100 concurrent user requests). The §5.7 multi-engine text gives no concurrency number; only the Fig. 14 x-axis shows a 0–100 concurrent-user-request sweep.
(2) Workload modes: there are four synthesized modes, not three: Poisson rate, offline batch, fixed concurrency and a custom arrival file. Replaying the exact traced arrivals is the default on top of these.
(3) turns_per_session: "Requests with more than 1000 LLM/tool calls are dropped" is wrong. The paper only observes that "The traces we collected in our evaluation contain no more than 1000 LLM/tool calls per user request". It describes no filter.
(4) output_tokens: this is partly stated, not "not stated". For mini-SWE-agent (§5.8), 4.5%, 12% and 13.5% of requests exceed 40K total output tokens across three traces.
(5) hardware_model: the default serving model for §5.3–5.5 is gpt-oss-120b. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is used only in §5.6/§5.7. CPU prefix caching needed a vLLM modification and was enabled only for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The vLLM version is v0.19.0. The two servers for §5.7 are joined by 100 Gbps InfiniBand.
(6) context_tokens: add §5.5, "an average of 40k context tokens" for DeerFlow against a serving KV capacity of about 213k tokens. Add that mini-SWE-agent prompts concatenate all prior LLM and tool I/O.
(7) inter_turn_gap: the text gives no tool-time statistics, but Figs. 9 and 13 do plot a "Tool" segment in the latency breakdown.
(8) The evidence quote for the Table 2 mini-SWE-agent row was reconstructed with numeric citation markers and is not verbatim. I replaced it with the Table 2 caption.
I also added rates and concurrency figures the record missed: mini-SWE-agent saturates at 4.5 req/min with about 24 running LLM calls; the Fig. 13 sweep covers 10–90 concurrent users; ODR averages 20.1 parallel search-and-summarize operations. evidence_quotes: First, XPerf can generate online serving workloads at a target request rate by sampling arrival times from a Poisson process.
Third, XPerf supports maintaining a fixed number of concurrent requests (i.e., fixed-concurrency serving) to synthesize a workload in which multiple users share one serving system
Finally, XPerf supports custom request arrival patterns, specified by a user-provided configuration file that lists each request ID and its arrival time.
By default, XPerf replays each request at the exact arrival time observed during tracing.
In fixed-concurrency setups, we maintain a fixed number of in-flight user requests for each application.
For throughput, mini-SWE-agent degrades by 35% as concurrency increases from 10 to 50, since higher concurrency causes prefix-cache thrashing.

DeerFlow shows the opposite trend, with throughput rising from 0.64 to 0.95 req/min as concurrency increases from 4 to 36, since more concurrent requests increase the decode batch size and there is no prefix-cache to thrash.

To demonstrate this, we use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with mini-SWE-agent to synthesize fixed-concurrency workloads. We scale the serving system from 1 to 4 engines, each holding one copy of the LLM, distributed across two of our testbed server machines.
Both scheduling policies achieve lower end-to-end latency (by 720 to 910 seconds under 100 concurrent requests) on trace 2 compared to traces 1 and 3.
For instance, with mini-SWE-agent, the number of running calls stabilizes at 24 on average, while the queue begins to grow once the request rate reaches 4.5 requests per minute.
Each measurement runs for two hours.
By default, XPerf treats tool-call durations as independent of serving system load, since tool calls typically execute on a separate machine.
When awoken, an LLM call node replays its LLM call and waits for the call to finish, while a tool call node further sleeps for the traced tool call duration to reproduce its latency.
Table 2. Agentic workloads used in our evaluation. LLM-call counts are per user request and profiled using gpt-oss-120b.
The traces we collected in our evaluation contain no more than 1000 LLM/tool calls per user request.
Prefill is most significant for DeerFlow, which has the longest LLM call input prompts among the studied applications (38.8k tokens on average).
DeerFlow saturates at a lower usage of around 75%, since its LLM calls have an average of 40k context tokens while our tested serving system has ∼213k token capacity.
Its LLM calls expose substantial opportunities for prefix-cache sharing: the prompt for each LLM call concatenates the inputs and outputs of all preceding LLM and tool calls.
This is because trace 2 contains fewer long requests with only 4.5% of requests exceeding 40K total output tokens, versus 12% and 13.5% for traces 1 and 3.
The server has two NVIDIA H100 NVL 94GB GPUs, each attached to the host through a PCIe Gen5 x16 link.
By default, we use gpt-oss-120b.
We apply minor modifications to vLLM to enable CPU prefix caching for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and output token ID enforcement.
For example, in mini-SWE-agent, each call reuses this context as its prefix, reaching 91% at low rates but falling below 4% as the rate rises.
Under KV cache pressure, an agent’s prefix cache may be evicted during tool calls, causing prefix-cache thrashing and reducing the hit rate.

Regarding KV cache management, InferCept (Abhyankar et al., 2024), Continuum (Li et al., 2025), CONCUR (Chen et al., 2026), and ThunderAgent (Kang et al., 2026) reduce recomputation overhead by preventing unnecessary cache evictions during tool calls, whereas KVFlow (Pan et al., 2025), PBKV (Zheng et al., 2026), and ScaleSim (Pan et al., 2026b) proactively swap the cache to CPU memory based on predicted execution in multi-agent workflows.
Open Deep Research (ODR) launches multiple web searches in parallel, each followed by an LLM call that summarizes its results; on average, 20.1 such search-and-summarize operations run concurrently.

result.corrections:
Most numbers match the sources. I made five corrections:
(1) inter_turn_gap means something different than the record says. In multi-round-qa.py, last_request_time is set when a request is launched, so gap_between_requests = num_users/qps is the time from one launch to the next for each user. It is not think time after a response. Think time is that gap minus the response latency. If the user's previous request has not finished, the next one waits and a warning is logged. The 10 users at 0.5 QPS = 20 s arithmetic is correct.
(2) The paper does not say that its multi-round Q&A workload uses the production-stack multi-round-qa.py benchmark. It mentions the vLLM production stack only as an adopter of the KV connector API, plus a reference. So the benchmark-code values are an inferred link, not the paper's stated setup. The two workloads also have different shapes. The paper describes each query as a ~10K-token document plus a question. The benchmark sends a system prompt and user info once and then resends the growing chat history.
(3) The paper and the code use "QPS" differently. The paper says users "join according to a specified arrival rate (QPS)". In the code, qps is the overall request rate, and users join every gap_between_users = (num_rounds-1)/qps seconds. In steady state, live sessions ≈ num_users.
(4) The 1-7.5 QPS range is only the Fig. 8 axis tick labels (2,4 / 2.5,5.0,7.5 / 1,2,3 / 2,4 / 2.5,5.0). The paper does not list the exact QPS values it swept.
(5) The Fig. 8 models also include Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct. Sao10K-L3-8B appears in the real-trace experiments. The source read is arXiv 2510.09665v2 (5 Dec 2025), and the benchmark read is production-stack main at commit 691dffa.

Checked against the arXiv HTML (arXiv:2609.02027v1 [cs.PF], 02 Sep 2026). Title, authors, hardware, N = 2,275, λ0 values, μF sweeps and the 5,000 + 1,000 conversation counts are all correct. Corrections:
(1) workload_type / inter_turn_gap: "think time" is the wrong label. The paper's W is the prompt-to-prompt interarrival time, measured between the submissions of turn j and turn j+1. The realized value is W = max{W_E2E, W_sample}, where W_sample ~ Exp(1/μF) and W_E2E is the time to finish decoding (eq. 80). So the exponential clock starts when the prompt is submitted and includes decode time. It is not a think time that starts after the response. The paper also says the realized mean μ̂F > μF for small μF, and μ̂F < μF for large μF because the finite horizon censors long gaps. μF = 135 s was chosen for Exp. 2 because its realized mean was closest to the target.
(2) turns_per_session: "the theory assumes geometric turn counts" is wrong. The general model (MCM) allows any i.i.d. positive-integer M. Geometric M is only one of the extra assumptions under which the MCM reduces to Zhang et al.'s SCM special case. The measured stats are stated: mean 4.4694, variance 7.9659, max 37, and 22,347 turns across the 5,000 measurement conversations. The conversations were sampled with at least 2 turns; the warm-up set is 1,000 conversations with 4,690 turns.
(3) context_tokens: tokens are not given directly, but E[B]-hat = 12.9220 KV blocks (lifetime cumulative per conversation) at 128 tokens per block, which is about 1.65K tokens (derived). Also A_R-hat = 38.9092 and A_H^hash-hat = 22.5178 blocks.
(4) output_tokens: made more precise. The decoder is forced to generate the same number of tokens as the recorded ShareGPT response, then the generated text and its response KV are discarded, and the original text is replayed.
(5) concurrent_sessions: correctly marked as not stated. A Little's-law estimate (mine, not the paper's) is λ0 × (E[M]−1) × μ̂F ≈ 1.5 × 3.47 × 135 ≈ 700 live conversations. That scales to about 235–940 over λ0 = 0.5–2.0.
(6) Added details: vLLM v0.22.1 + vLLM-Ascend v0.22.1rc1 + Mooncake v0.3.9. Each block is 18 MB (144 KB/token × 128). vLLM's LRU differs from the model in these ways: recency is set by P→D transfer, CPU DRAM write-back and prefill access; blocks with a nonzero refcount are protected from eviction; eviction keeps the prefix and drops the suffix first.

result.corrections:
None of the numeric fields is wrong. Every value appears in the README, generate_multi_turn.json, benchmark_serving_multi_turn.py or bench_dataset.py on main (fetched 2026-09-23). The file was first added on 2025-08-08 in PR #20267, so the year 2025 is correct. Five points make the record more precise:
(1) turns_per_session: input_num_turns in the README table counts the messages in each request (the code sets input_num_turns=len(messages)), not user turns. The values are always odd, so a max of 17 means the 9th user turn with 16 earlier messages, and a mean of 7.43 means about the 4th user turn on average. The turn count is drawn as a uniform integer from 12 to 18 and rounded up to even, so the only outcomes are 12, 14, 16 or 18 messages (12 has probability 1/7, each of the others 2/7). That gives 6 to 9 user turns, as the record says.
(2) concurrent_sessions: --max-active-conversations is split evenly across clients by integer division (max_active_conversations // num_clients), so the README example gives each client 3 conversations. When the flag is not set it defaults to num_clients, which means one active conversation per client. The number of requests in flight is at most num_clients, and it is lower while clients sleep between requests (request-rate > 0).
(3) inter_turn_gap: the Poisson sleep runs after every request a client sends, not once per conversation turn. With k active conversations per client in round-robin order, one conversation's gap is the latencies of the other k-1 requests plus k exponential sleeps with mean 1/rate. There is also a --conversation-sampling random option; round-robin is the default.
(4) arrival_or_rate: the README example run is closed-loop at 0.769 req/s, with 166 requests over 215.81 s.
(5) kv_mechanism_relevance: the tool only generates load and has no KV prefetch, pinning, TTL or eviction logic of its own. The phrase "cleanest concurrency definition among tools surveyed" is the extractor's opinion, not a claim the source makes.

verified.workload_type: Synthetic multi-turn Q&A conversations generated from a text file (pg1184.txt), or ShareGPT conversations converted with convert_sharegpt_to_openai.py (README example uses 128 of them), for KV-offload benchmarking
verified.concurrent_sessions: There are two knobs. (a) --num-clients: the number of parallel client processes. Each client runs one async loop that awaits one request at a time, so this sets the maximum number of requests in flight. (b) --max-active-conversations: the number of live conversations across all clients, split per client as max_active // num_clients. It defaults to num_clients, which gives one conversation per client. The README example uses 2 clients and 6 active conversations, so each client holds 3 and at most 2 requests are in flight. The example config generates 24 conversations in total.
verified.arrival_or_rate: --request-rate is a Poisson rate per client (an exponential sleep with mean 1/rate after each request). The default of 0 means no delay, so the loop is closed. The README example run measured requests_per_sec = 0.769, with 166 requests in 215.81 s.
verified.inter_turn_gap: There is no explicit think time. Each client serves its k = max_active/num_clients conversations in round-robin order by default (random order is an option). A conversation's gap between turns is therefore the end-to-end latency of the other k-1 conversations' requests on the same client. When request-rate > 0 it also includes k exponential sleeps with mean 1/rate, one after each request, including the conversation's own.
verified.turns_per_session: Example config: num_turns (user plus assistant messages) is a uniform integer from 12 to 18, rounded up to even, so each conversation has 12, 14, 16 or 18 messages, which is 6 to 9 user turns. README output: input_num_turns (the number of messages in each request, always odd) has mean 7.43 and max 17. The max corresponds to the 9th user turn. The --max-turns flag can cap messages per conversation.
verified.context_tokens: Example config: a 500-token common prefix shared by all conversations and prepended to the first user turn; a per-conversation prefix drawn from a lognormal with average 1000 and max 5000, added to the first user turn only; each user message a uniform 120 to 160 tokens. README run: input_num_tokens mean 2006.20, median 2019, p99 3736.45, max 3899, min 522.
verified.output_tokens: Example config: a uniform 80 to 120 tokens per assistant message. README run: output_num_tokens mean 100.01, max 120. The --limit-min-tokens and --limit-max-tokens flags can override this.
verified.hardware_model: Hardware not stated. The README example serves Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with vllm serve.
verified.kv_mechanism_relevance: Generic load generator whose stated purpose is benchmarking KV-cache offloading. It implements no prefetch, pinning, TTL or eviction itself. For KV-tiering work it is useful because it keeps the number of resident live sessions (max-active-conversations) separate from the number of requests in flight (num-clients). The idle time between a session's turns is set by round-robin over the other sessions on the same client, plus optional Poisson sleeps. Varying the active-conversations to clients ratio therefore directly controls how long each session's KV sits idle and has to survive in a lower tier.

verified.workload_type: Trace-driven prefix-cache simulation. Multi-turn chat traces from LMSys-Chat-1M and ShareGPT, plus agent traces from SWE-agent/SWE-bench (the artifact uses the 20240820_honeycomb SWE-bench Verified trajectories). All traces are tokenized with the Llama-2-7b tokenizer.

verified.arrival_or_rate: Session arrival rate. The artifact sweeps sessions_per_second over {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10} and generates traces at every rate. Start times are deterministic and evenly spaced, not a Poisson process.

The LMSys check is history + user input + output > 32768; the ShareGPT and SWE-bench check is history + user input > 32768. SWE-bench history collapses environment observations older than the last 5 rounds. Paper: SWE-bench inputs range 'from hundreds of tokens to tens of thousands'; LMSys mostly under 10K; ShareGPT mostly under 2K.

verified.kv_mechanism_relevance: Admission and eviction for a single prefix cache holding hybrid (SSM + KV) states. Entries are admitted by estimated reuse likelihood and evicted by a FLOP-efficiency-weighted score (compute saved per byte) combined with recency, with alpha tuned by grid search. There is no prefetch, no multi-tier offload, and no TTL/pinning around idle or tool time. The paper cites CachedAttention and Pensieve only as hierarchical-cache related work. What transfers to KV tiering: the finding that longer intra-session gaps and higher session arrival rates lower hit rate but widen the benefit of cost-aware eviction over LRU.
evidence_quotes: These datasets contain multiple chat sessions, each with multiple rounds of requests. We vary the inter-session arrival time and inter-request arrival time to account for environment response time (e.g., human typing, interactions with the coding IDE) and queuing delay in the inference engine.

As the average number of request (chat) sessions per second increases from 0.5 to 2, Marconi's token hit rate decreases from 48.7% to 43.0%. Similarly, as the average response time between requests in a session increases from 5 s to 10 s, Marconi's token hit rate decreases from 25.9% to 24.1%
We vary the cache size from 60 GB (high contention) to 140 GB (low contention).
We use a 7B Hybrid model with {4,24,28} {Attention,SSM,MLP} layers in our main results.
Experiments were run on a p4d.24xlarge AWS instance with eight A100-40GB GPUs, 96 Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8275CL CPUs, and 1152GB of DDR4 RAM.
The LLM output sequences in LMSys are relatively long, often reaching thousands of tokens, whereas the LLM output sequences in ShareGPT are succinct and often take tens or hundreds of tokens.

SWEBench has the widest input sequence length distribution, ranging from hundreds of tokens to tens of thousands of tokens. LMSys has a narrower distribution, with most sequences under 10K tokens, while ShareGPT predominantly features sequences under 2K tokens.

result.name: C80 x 50 turns, TraceLab tool+think gaps (smallest load that reaches the SSD)
result.gap_model: Each (conv, turn>0) gets a deterministic, seeded gap. It is written into a derived trace with pre_gap overwritten and replayed with GAP=1 and GAP_CAP=0, so all 4 arms sleep the same gap on the same turn. Do not use --gap-sample: it draws from one shared RNG in completion order, so the sequence differs between arms. The gap is still measured from the end of the reply. It has two parts. (1) Tool time, drawn every turn: min(216 s, LogNormal(median 0.3 s, p90 13.6 s)), sigma 2.98. That is TraceLab Table 7 tool latency, capped at its p99 of 3.6 min; capped mean 8.5 s. (2) Think time, added with probability p = 1/8.8 = 0.114 (TraceLab: 8.8 LLM calls per user request): min(1,800 s, LogNormal(median 84 s, p90 1,236 s)), sigma 2.10. That is TraceLab human think time. The 30-min cap keeps about 93% of these gaps unchanged; the capped mean is 328 s. Resulting per-turn gap: p10 0.01 s, p50 0.49 s, p75 5.6 s, p90 61 s, p95 216 s, p99 1,456 s, mean 45.9 s. 10% of gaps exceed 1 min, 3.2% exceed 5 min, 2.0% exceed 10 min and 1.2% exceed 20 min. The trace's own pre_gap at x1 (p50 0.71 s, mean 2.08 s) has almost the same median as the tool part. It does not work alone because it has no think tail: at any load this box can sustain, the SSD is never reached (see the arithmetic).
result.arrival_model: Session arrivals start as a Poisson ramp at 0.1 conversations/s (ARRIVAL=0.1), capped at 80 live (--concurrency 80). The 80 slots fill in about 13 min. After that it is a closed loop: a session holds its slot across its gaps, and a finished session is replaced at once by the next unused conversation. The pool is the 228 trace conversations with exactly 50 turns (TURNS=50), each used at most once per arm, since the client cannot bust the cache. Per-arm wall cap is MAX_SECONDS=7200; the pool runs dry at about 2 h anyway. Analysis window: 15 to 120 min. Pair turns across arms by (conv, turn), and read the tier effect by deterministic gap class (for example gap >= 10 min), not by the tier each arm happened to observe.
result.conversation_selection: Use the 228 conversations with exactly 50 turns (of 768), in trace order, OFFSET=0. Put them in the same derived trace file that carries the deterministic gaps, because replay_agentic.py has no min-turns filter. Every session builds up its full history. Context p50 at turns 1 / 10 / 20 / 40 / 50: 9.9K / 18.8K / 25.3K / 37.3K / 43.7K tokens. Final context mean 45.6K (p10 35K, p90 57.6K). The 7,808-token system prompt is shared by all sessions. Private KV per session: 21.3K tokens averaged over its lifetime, about 37.8K at turn 50. Caveat: these are the long SWE-bench tasks that used up the 50-step budget, so the pool is biased toward long tasks.
result.expected_utilization: These are predictions. Three-tier arms: about 0.6 of GPU capacity (1.35 turns/s x 0.45 GPU-s per hit turn). At x70 the three-tier arm stayed stable at 1.8 turns/s in its steady window, so there is margin. hbm_host: about 0.8, because 2.5% of returns recompute about 29K tokens at about 6.3 s each; across seeds the range is 0.77 to 0.87. hbm_lru: about 1.4, because 10% of returns recompute. The closed loop then throttles it to about 1.0 turns/s, which adds about 20 s of queueing per turn (80/0.97 - 60 s cycle). That is mild overload, not the 100-150 s queues of x10/x1. SSD: about 5% read-busy (0.03 restores/s x ~2.9 GB) and about 8% write-busy (write-through of ~1.1K new tokens per turn, about 0.15 GB/s). Running requests take about 12 x 30K = 0.37M of the 668K-token L1.
result.expected_L3_reach: About 2.5% of returning turns (range 2.2-2.7% across seeds) have their prefix only on the SSD. That is about 190 SSD restores per arm in the 15-120 min window, out of about 8,400 steady turns. About 8% come from L2 (about 650) and about 90% from L1. The split follows the gap classes. L1 returns come after tool gaps (gap p50 0.3 s, p90 12 s). L2 returns come after think gaps with p50 of about 2-3 min (p10 1 min, p90 6 min). SSD returns come after think gaps with p50 of about 15-22 min (p10 about 10 min). A long gap reaches the SSD because the LRU distance during it covers the whole live set (80 x 21.3K = 1.70M, which is at least L2 = 1.63M) plus the KV of sessions that finished during the gap. This matches TraceLab's measured pattern: misses begin at gaps over 5 min, and nearly everything misses past 1 h. The model is calibrated on the x70 campaign. There it predicted L1/L2/L3 of .28/.49/.22 and 1.93 turns/s, against measured .25/.49/.24 and 1.8 turns/s in the steady window. Sensitivity: L2 10% smaller gives L3 3.1%; C=64 gives 1.7%; C=96 gives 2.7-3.0%.
literature_anchors: TraceLab (arXiv 2606.30560, UW, 4,265 Claude Code/Codex sessions, 357K LLM steps). Table 7 tool latency: p50 0.3 s, p90 13.6 s, p99 3.6 min, mean 18.4 s. Human think: p50 1.4 min, p90 20.6 min. 8.8 LLM calls per user request. Global prefix-cache hit rate 95.7%. Misses start at gaps over 5 min, and nearly every step misses past 1 h. Gives the tool+think mixture, p = 1/8.8, and the gap classes.

Anchors the closed loop with replacement and the C range.
